#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report (WNGSR)
Description: The Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report is the U.S. government’s only Principal Federal Economic Indicator that provides weekly data; other indicators report either monthly or quarterly data. WNGSR reports the underground working natural gas storage level as of the previous Friday, weekly net change, comparisons to historical levels and net changes, and statistical measures for each of five regions in the Lower 48 states.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report (WNGSR)

**Research checked:** October 9, 2026  
**Publisher:** U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), U.S. Department of Energy (DOE)  
**Official report:** [Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/ngs.html)

## Executive assessment

The WNGSR is a free, publicly available, market-sensitive statistical report estimating **working natural gas held in underground storage in the contiguous United States**. It is important infrastructure for monitoring fuel availability, interpreting natural gas prices, planning for seasonal demand, and overseeing energy markets.

Your description is substantially accurate and closely matches [EIA’s own description](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=43335). Several qualifications are essential:

- **“Principal Federal Economic Indicator” is a formal designation**, not a general description of every federal economic dataset. EIA describes WNGSR as the only weekly indicator in that designated class; this does **not** mean it is the government’s only weekly economic report.
- Its figures are **statistical estimates**, not a weekly census of every storage facility.
- It reports five regions **and a Lower 48 total**, with additional **salt and nonsalt storage subdivisions for South Central**.
- **Net inventory change is not always physical gas flow.** Reclassifications between working and base gas can change reported inventories without an equivalent injection or withdrawal.
- The current historical database is a **revised, latest-estimate series**, not an immutable record of what the public knew at every original release.
- Historical coverage depends on the product: the legacy three-region archive begins **December 31, 1993**; the current five-region API and time-series table inspected begin **January 1, 2010**.

**Preservation conclusion:** Preserve the report as a collection—data, release text, uncertainty estimates, revisions, methodology, geography, survey instruments, and governance records—not merely as a single inventory time series.

---

## 1. Dataset identity and contents

| Attribute | Findings |
|---|---|
| Public product title | **Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report** |
| Acronym | **WNGSR** |
| Main collection instrument | **Form EIA-912, Weekly Underground Natural Gas Storage Report** |
| Supporting collection | **Form EIA-191**, the monthly underground-storage census |
| Subject | Working natural gas inventories in underground storage |
| Geographic scope | Lower 48 states; five EIA storage regions |
| Frequency | Weekly |
| Reference time | Friday morning; survey documentation specifies **9:00 a.m. Central Standard Time** |
| Ordinary publication time | Following Thursday, **10:30 a.m. Eastern Time** |
| Holiday exceptions | Published in the official [release schedule](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/schedule.html) |
| Published volume unit | **Billion cubic feet (Bcf)** |
| Survey reporting unit | **Million cubic feet (MMcf)**; survey forms specify standardized pressure and temperature |
| Access | Free web publication and downloads; EIA API access uses a free registration key |
| Data type | Aggregated statistical time series, not publicly released respondent microdata |

### Main reported variables

The report includes:

- Current and previous week’s working gas stocks.
- Weekly net change.
- **Implied flow**, distinguishing reportable reclassifications from inventory change.
- Year-ago stocks and percentage comparisons.
- Five-year average stocks and percentage comparisons.
- Historical minimum–maximum range.
- **Coefficients of variation for stock estimates**.
- **Standard errors for weekly net changes**.
- Revision and reclassification notes or flags when applicable.

The main inventory table has eight geographic/storage categories: Lower 48 total, five regions, and the two South Central subdivisions. **Do not add the South Central total and its subdivisions together.**

Sources: [report](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/ngs.html), [notes](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/notes.html), [methodology](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/methodology.html).

### What “working gas” means

Working gas is inventory in addition to **base or cushion gas**, which supports the operation and pressure of a storage reservoir. Underground facilities include depleted oil and gas reservoirs, aquifers, and salt caverns.

Working inventories should not be confused with:

- Total gas physically present, including cushion gas.
- Maximum storage capacity.
- Proven natural gas reserves.
- Pipeline linepack.
- Production or consumption.
- The rate at which gas can actually be delivered to customers.

A large inventory does not, by itself, guarantee adequate local supply: withdrawal capability, pipeline constraints, weather, and facility availability also matter.

---

## 2. Publisher, authority, and mandate

### Institutional responsibility

EIA produces and disseminates the report within DOE. It is a statistical agency, not the energy-market regulator.

EIA’s [legislative history](https://www.eia.gov/about/legislative_timeline.php) explains that the DOE Organization Act gave it independence from DOE regarding data collection and from the government regarding the content of its reports. This distinction matters when evaluating political influence: **EIA statistics are not supposed to be policy advocacy by DOE.**

### Statutory foundations

The relevant authorities are broader energy-information laws rather than a statute prescribing every detail of a Thursday storage release:

1. **Federal Energy Administration Act of 1974**, Public Law 93-275.  
   Establishes energy-information collection and enforcement authority. Form EIA-912 reporting is mandatory under **15 U.S.C. §772(b)**.

2. **Energy Conservation and Production Act of 1976**.  
   Established the predecessor energy-information office and a comprehensive national energy-information system.

3. **Department of Energy Organization Act of 1977**, including **42 U.S.C. §7135**.  
   Established EIA and its institutional independence.

An early WNGSR [Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2002-07-11/html/02-17421.htm) explicitly connects the report to EIA’s mandate to collect, analyze, and disseminate information needed to assess near- and longer-term energy-resource adequacy.

### Paperwork Reduction Act and OMB approval

The collection belongs to the **Natural Gas Data Collection Program**, under:

- **OMB control number:** 1905-0175.
- **Information Collection Request:** 202404-1905-001.
- **Approval date:** July 12, 2024.
- **Expiration date:** July 31, 2027.

The approval record identifies statutory collection authorities and documents public-comment proceedings. See the [official OMB/OIRA record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202404-1905-001); an accessible [mirror](https://omb.report/icr/202404-1905-001) reproduces its details.

**Important budget caveat:** Costs and burden totals for this package cover multiple natural gas surveys. They should not be attributed entirely to WNGSR.

### Principal Federal Economic Indicator status

EIA’s supporting statement says WNGSR was designated a **Principal Federal Economic Indicator in January 2008**. The designation reflects its importance as a timely signal of readily available natural gas supply and its influence on spot and futures markets.

The report is subject to **OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 3**, including requirements concerning documentation, timely release, prevention of premature disclosure, and performance assessment.

EIA states that agencies issuing these indicators must report on performance every three years. Its [performance-evaluation page](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/evaluation.html) lists evaluations covering 2008–2010 through 2020–2022; the latest listed evaluation was released in November 2024.

Source for designation and documented regulatory uses: [EIA supporting statement](https://omb.report/icr/202012-1905-001/doc/106700200.pdf).

---

## 3. History and significant changes

| Date or period | Development and significance |
|---|---|
| **1994** | American Gas Association (AGA) began publishing weekly storage estimates. |
| **October 2001** | AGA announced it would discontinue the survey because of resource constraints. |
| **March 15, 2002** | First reference week for EIA’s weekly survey collection; responses were due March 18. |
| **May 1, 2002** | AGA’s final release, covering April 26. |
| **May 9, 2002** | EIA’s first public WNGSR release, covering May 3. |
| **2003** | EIA changed estimation, expanded the sample, and revised a 17-week historical interval. |
| **January 2005** | Historical comparisons switched to daily interpolation for matching calendar dates. |
| **August 2005** | Revised sampling and estimation approach introduced. |
| **January 2008** | PFEI designation, according to EIA’s supporting statement. |
| **2015** | Transition from three regions to five; historical five-region estimates reconstructed from 2010. |
| **November 16, 2015** | Special release replaced the November 6 three-region report with five-region data. |
| **November 19, 2015** | First normal release of a new reporting week in five-region format. |
| **2015** | Revision/reclassification publication threshold reduced from 7 Bcf to 4 Bcf. |
| **2018** | Explicit South Central salt/nonsalt collection; Pacific census coverage; updated rounding treatment. |
| **December 28, 2020** | HTTPS became required for automated retrieval of key release products. |
| **2026** | Related Natural Gas Weekly Update ended; WNGSR Supplement launched as a separate afternoon analytical product. |

Sources: [methodology](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/methodology.html), [monthly–weekly differences](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/mthdiff.html), [region-transition FAQ](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/faqregions.html), [HTTPS notice](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/notice.html?src=home-b1), [final Weekly Update](https://www.eia.gov/naturalgas/weekly/).

### Historical data are not uniform in origin

The early history contains reconstructed estimates:

- December 31, 1993 is based on EIA monthly data.
- Most of January 1994–February 2002 combines EIA monthly information with AGA weekly information.
- The transition in March 2002 includes interpolation.
- From March 15, 2002 onward, the history is based on EIA’s weekly collection.

Similarly, five-region data for January 2010–June 12, 2015 were reconstructed from information originally collected under the older regional system. EIA began generating estimates from respondent data for the new five regions with June 19, 2015 data.

**Analytical implication:** Historical rows should carry provenance and methodology-period labels. A reconstructed observation is not equivalent to a contemporaneously published five-region survey estimate.

### Documentation discrepancies worth preserving

Official sources are not perfectly consistent:

- A [2011 explanatory article](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=3370) says the report was first released in March 2002. Detailed methodology distinguishes **March collection** from **May public publication**.
- A [2023 explanatory article](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=56900) says five-region history goes back to 2006. The current API metadata and time-series table inspected begin in **2010**.
- The 2015 regional FAQ and 2018 methodology describe rounding implementation differently.

For cataloging, prefer the detailed methodology and the actual coverage of the downloaded artifact. Preserve conflicting statements rather than silently “correcting” the historical record.

---

## 4. Geographic coverage

These are **EIA storage regions**, not Census regions, utility service territories, or pipeline networks.

| Region | Included jurisdictions |
|---|---|
| **East** | CT, DE, DC, FL, GA, MA, MD, ME, NH, NJ, NY, NC, OH, PA, RI, SC, VT, VA, WV |
| **Midwest** | IL, IN, IA, KY, MI, MN, MO, TN, WI |
| **South Central** | AL, AR, KS, LA, MS, OK, TX |
| **Mountain** | AZ, CO, ID, MT, NE, ND, NM, NV, SD, UT, WY |
| **Pacific** | CA, OR, WA |

Alaska, Hawaii, and U.S. territories are outside the headline Lower 48 series.

The old regions—**East, West, and Producing**—cannot be converted to the current regions by simply splitting columns. State assignments changed: for example, New Mexico moved to Mountain, Minnesota to Midwest, and Nebraska to Mountain.

Sources: [regional definitions](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/notes.html), [transition FAQ](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/faqregions.html).

---

## 5. How the estimates are produced

### Survey design

EIA uses the monthly EIA-191 census as the sampling frame for weekly EIA-912 reporting.

The published methodology describes:

- Six strata: East, Midwest, Mountain, Pacific, South Central Salt, South Central Nonsalt.
- Selection with **probability proportional to size** for noncertainty operators.
- Certain large operators and operators crossing strata selected with certainty.
- A target relative standard error no greater than **5% in each stratum**.
- Approximately **80–85 weekly respondents** in the 2018 methodology, typically covering at least 90% of storage volumes within a stratum.
- Full weekly census coverage of Pacific operators beginning with the 2018 sample.
- Sample reselection typically every two to three years.

These are dated methodological descriptions, **not a verified 2026 respondent count**. Also, storage-volume coverage and storage-capacity coverage are different measures; EIA explanatory articles citing about 95% capacity coverage should not be treated as identical to the methodology’s volume-coverage figure.

### Estimation and imputation

The estimator combines:

1. Reported weekly stocks from sampled operators.
2. Each operator’s historical monthly storage behavior.
3. A 12-month moving average based on monthly information, available with a lag.
4. Weekly behavior of sampled operators within the corresponding stratum.
5. Adjustments for changes such as facility startups, shutdowns, ownership changes, and gas reclassifications.

Missing or questionable responses can be imputed using stratum trends or treatment similar to nonsampled operators.

### Validation

EIA compares submissions with recent weekly data, monthly records, weather, pipeline flows, and other estimates. Staff contact respondents to confirm or correct unusual values.

Source: [methodology](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/methodology.html).

### Collection scope versus publication scope

Some later EIA-912 instructions also mention **marine terminals operating LNG storage**. That does not establish that those inventories are included in the published underground working-gas totals.

For a data dictionary, distinguish:

- What a particular survey-instrument version requests.
- What the headline WNGSR series actually measures.
- Any separately published LNG product.

Do not redefine WNGSR as total U.S. underground-plus-LNG inventory based solely on survey instructions.

---

## 6. Quality, uncertainty, and interpretation

### Sampling uncertainty

EIA publishes:

- **Stock coefficient of variation (CV)**, expressed as a percentage.
- **Net-change standard error (SE)**, expressed in Bcf.

Its methodology uses **1,000 bootstrap replicates**, with a finite-population correction. Net-change uncertainty accounts for covariance between successive stock estimates.

Consequently:

- Do not sum regional standard errors.
- Do not derive net-change uncertainty by assuming successive stock estimates are independent.
- A zero Pacific sampling-error estimate does **not** mean zero reporting, coverage, or processing error.

Sampling-variability history is available from the week ending **April 10, 2015**.

For approximate confidence intervals:

\[
SE_{\text{stocks}} = \text{stocks}\times CV/100
\]

A conventional approximate 95% interval is the estimate ±1.96 SE, with EIA’s documented rounding conventions. These intervals do not capture every source of survey error.

Sources: [methodology](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/methodology.html), [possible survey errors](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/possiblesurveyerrors.html).

### Monthly benchmarking

EIA compares interpolated weekly month-end estimates with its monthly census.

The comparison page updated October 8, 2026 reports an average absolute difference of approximately **11 Bcf, or 0.4%**, for January 2010–July 2026.

This is useful evidence of agreement, but **not** a claim that every weekly observation is accurate within 0.4%. The comparison also reflects timing, interpolation, reporting differences, and revisions.

Source: [monthly–weekly comparison](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/mthdiff.html).

### Historical comparisons are interpolated

Since January 2005, EIA has used daily linear interpolation to match calendar dates across years.

Therefore:

- “Year ago” can differ from the value published for the nearest Friday in the previous year.
- Five-year statistics are not necessarily simple averages of identically numbered reporting weeks.
- Regional historical minima and maxima need not sum to the national minimum or maximum.
- The five-year shaded range is **not a confidence interval**.
- The five-year average is a moving historical baseline, not a forecast or a weather-normalized measure.

### Inventory change versus physical flow

Net change reflects all events changing working inventories, including reclassification.

**Implied flow excludes reportable reclassifications totaling 4 Bcf or more**, but EIA cautions that smaller unpublished net revisions may remain in it.

For physical-flow analysis, use implied flow where available, retain notes, and avoid presenting inventory differences as perfectly measured injections or withdrawals.

---

## 7. Revisions and real-time information

Under the published [revision policy](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/revisions.html):

- Ordinary published revisions occur when respondent-reported changes reach **4 Bcf** at a regional or Lower 48 level.
- When a revision is published, changes to all affected regions are recorded.
- Qualifying changes of **10 Bcf or more** involving the two most recent reporting weeks can trigger an out-of-cycle release.
- Out-of-cycle releases occur on a federal workday at **2:00 p.m. Eastern**, following public notice between 1:00 and 1:10 p.m.
- Methodology changes are announced separately.
- Reclassifications are reported in regularly scheduled releases rather than through the out-of-cycle procedure.
- Historical inventory and uncertainty files contain the latest available estimates and may be revised.

EIA maintains [revision and reclassification history](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/revisions.xls), including original estimates and accompanying notes.

**For event studies and backtesting:** A current historical download is not necessarily the information available to a trader or regulator on the original release date. Use original releases or preserved vintages to prevent look-ahead bias.

---

## 8. Typical users and benefits to the public

### Documented users

EIA identifies policymakers, commodity-market analysts, and industry experts as users.

Its supporting statement documents specific **FERC** uses:

- Assessing supply tightness and market fundamentals.
- Winter and summer seasonal assessments.
- State-of-the-market reporting.
- Tracking injections, withdrawals, and price effects.
- Screening unusual price movements around storage announcements.

Sources: [2002 Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2002-07-11/html/02-17421.htm), [supporting statement](https://omb.report/icr/202012-1905-001/doc/106700200.pdf).

### Other major user groups and applications

| User group | Applications |
|---|---|
| Utilities and gas purchasers | Procurement, seasonal planning, inventory-risk assessment |
| Producers, pipelines, storage operators | Market assessment and operational planning |
| Traders, investors, risk managers | Supply-demand interpretation, hedging, announcement analysis |
| Researchers and data scientists | Forecasting, econometrics, weather-response models, regional comparisons |
| Journalists and educators | Explaining fuel availability, price changes, and seasonal conditions |
| Consumer and policy organizations | Evaluating claims about shortages, export pressures, infrastructure, and affordability |

### Public benefits

1. **An open benchmark:** Smaller firms, researchers, and the public can access a common reference without buying proprietary estimates.
2. **Supply monitoring:** Weekly information arrives much sooner than monthly census data.
3. **Market transparency:** Published methodology, uncertainty, and scheduled releases support scrutiny of an influential market signal.
4. **Regulatory oversight:** FERC’s documented uses connect the statistics to market surveillance.
5. **Public accountability:** Independent data help test claims about shortages and the need for particular policies or investments.
6. **Historical continuity:** EIA maintained the series after the industry association withdrew.

These are plausible and documented functions of the data. They are **not evidence that publication necessarily lowers household bills or prevents shortages**; those outcomes depend on many additional factors.

### Limits for policy advocacy

WNGSR cannot alone establish:

- Why a household’s bill rose.
- Whether a particular pipeline is necessary.
- Whether LNG exports caused a price movement.
- Facility-level methane leakage or safety.
- Distribution of energy insecurity across communities.
- Whether a particular operator manipulated the market.

Those questions require additional price, production, trade, infrastructure, weather, emissions, or household data.

---

## 9. Access, formats, and machine-readable identifiers

### Official release and historical files

| Resource | Official location |
|---|---|
| Current report | [ngs.html](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/ngs.html) |
| Current CSV | [wngsr.csv](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/wngsr.csv) |
| Current JSON | [wngsr.json](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/wngsr.json) |
| Summary text | [wngsr.txt](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/wngsr.txt) |
| Inventory history | [ngshistory.xls](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/ngshistory.xls) |
| Historical comparisons | [ngsstats.xls](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/ngsstats.xls) |
| Sampling variability history | [cvhistory.xls](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/cvhistory.xls) |
| Revision/reclassification history | [revisions.xls](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/revisions.xls) |
| Monthly–weekly differences | [mthdiff_history.xls](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/mthdiff_history.xls) |
| Legacy three-region history | [archngshistory.xls](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/archngshistory.xls) |

The [notes page](https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/notes.html#threeregion) links additional legacy comparison and revision files.

### API

The verified API route is:

```text
https://api.eia.gov/v2/natural-gas/stor/wkly/data/
```

Its metadata identifies weekly frequency, ISO-style dates, and facets for geography, product, process, and series.

Examples of current series identifiers:

| Series | Identifier |
|---|---|
| Lower 48 working gas | `NW2_EPG0_SWO_R48_BCF` |
| East | `NW2_EPG0_SWO_R31_BCF` |
| Midwest | `NW2_EPG0_SWO_R32_BCF` |

### Parsing hazards observed

The inspected release JSON and API responses reveal useful implementation details:

- API numeric values can arrive as **strings**.
- Release-JSON flags can be strings such as `"false"`, not Boolean values.
- The release JSON’s `release_date` contained **midnight**, while the HTML reported the actual **10:30 a.m.** publication time.
- Current-release JSON contains selected dates and comparisons; it is **not the complete history**.
- Uncertainty statistics are separate from the inspected release JSON.
- Region labels and geography metadata should be validated against the official region table.

For announcement studies, preserve the actual publication timestamp separately from the JSON date field.

## 10. Confidentiality, rights, and reproducibility

### Confidential respondent data

EIA-912 responses are protected under the **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA)** and applicable federal law. Identifiable responses are for statistical purposes and are not publicly disclosed without consent.

EIA’s regional FAQ states that it cannot provide identifiable weekly respondent information. Some monthly operator, location, and capacity information is publicly accessible under different disclosure rules.

**Consequence:** Public users can examine methodology and aggregate performance, but cannot fully reproduce the estimates from confidential operator-level inputs.

### Reuse rights

EIA’s [copyright and reuse policy](https://www.eia.gov/about/copyrights_reuse.php) permits use and redistribution of its public-domain government information products and asks for source acknowledgment including publication date.

Distinguish the numerical dataset from:

- EIA’s protected logo.
- Licensed photographs.
- Third-party material in related analytical products.

Suggested citation:

> U.S. Energy Information Administration. *Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report*, week ending [date], released [date and time]. [URL]. Retrieved [date]. [Original-release or revised-history version].

---

## 11. Preservation and cataloging recommendations

The following are recommendations, not claims that EIA already implements every practice.

### Preserve the complete evidence package

For each release, capture:

1. HTML report and summary text.
2. CSV and JSON.
3. Charts and relevant linked assets.
4. Historical inventory, comparison, and uncertainty spreadsheets.
5. Revision/reclassification files.
6. Release schedule and special notices.
7. Methodology, definitions, regional map, and error documentation.
8. Survey forms, instructions, OMB approvals, and Federal Register notices.
9. Periodic performance evaluations.

### Maintain two separate collections

- **Release-vintage collection:** What was published at a specific time.
- **Latest-revised collection:** EIA’s current best estimates.

Do not overwrite the former when refreshing the latter.

### Preserve originals and usable derivatives

Keep original XLS, JSON, HTML, and other files. Create documented UTF-8 CSV or Parquet derivatives for long-term use.

Record:

- Retrieval time in UTC.
- Report reference date.
- Release date and time.
- Original and final redirected URLs.
- File size, format, and checksum.
- Series identifier and units.
- Geographic-definition version.
- Revision/reclassification status.
- Transformation code and software versions.

During this research, some official URLs redirected to signed, time-limited delivery URLs. Cite the stable public address, while retaining redirect information in preservation metadata.

### Specific risks

- **Overwritten current-release files.**
- **Revised historical files that erase earlier vintages.**
- **Legacy spreadsheets and links.**
- **Methodology equations stored as images**, which text-only crawls may omit.
- **Documentation inconsistencies and stale dates.**
- **Dependence on the monthly census**, even though the public product is weekly.
- **Changes to related products**, such as the 2026 replacement of the Weekly Update.

I did not establish a WNGSR-specific permanent retention schedule, dedicated DOI, complete public archive of every release vintage, or standalone operating budget. Those are useful follow-up questions for EIA and federal records officials.

---

## 12. Priorities for data scientists and policy advocates

### For analysis

- Separate reference dates from information-availability dates.
- Retain original vintages for forecasting and event studies.
- Respect methodology and regional breaks.
- Use published implied flow rather than automatically equating stock change with physical flow.
- Retain uncertainty measures and revision notes.
- Allow for independent rounding.
- Model seasonality and weather explicitly.
- Do not interpret the five-year average as weather-normalized or causally explanatory.
- Pair inventories with capacity, deliverability, prices, production, consumption, and trade data as needed.

### For public-interest oversight

Useful questions include:

- Are release vintages preserved and accessible without commercial subscriptions?
- Are CSV, JSON, HTML, spreadsheets, and API data consistent?
- Are uncertainty and revision histories as accessible as headline inventories?
- Is the methodology updated to reflect current sampling practice?
- Are format changes and unusual revisions announced clearly?
- Is funding sufficient for both weekly collection and the monthly sampling frame?
- Can greater aggregate detail be published without compromising confidentiality?

Formal participation channels include Paperwork Reduction Act notices, EIA product consultations, and [information-quality procedures](https://www.eia.gov/about/information_quality_guidelines.php).

## Bottom line

**WNGSR is a high-priority preservation target because it records both physical energy conditions and market-moving public information.** Its principal strengths are timeliness, free access, statutory collection authority, institutional statistical independence, published methodology, uncertainty measures, and documented regulatory use.

Its central limitations are aggregation, confidential inputs, estimation error, historical reconstruction, changing regional definitions, and revisions. A trustworthy archive or analysis must preserve those qualifications alongside the headline numbers.

# WNGSR dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**  
**Scope:** The core **Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report (WNGSR)**, its underlying EIA-912 collection, and its public historical data—not every EIA natural gas publication.

## Overall finding

**WNGSR remains available and operational, but its continuity faces meaningful staffing and technical risks.** I found no evidence that its historical inventory series has been deliberately removed, that weekly collection has stopped, or that its current regional detail has been reduced.

The strongest warning signs are substantial EIA staff losses, a documented late WNGSR release, and agency-wide plans to consolidate products. Countervailing protections include active collection approval, statutory authority, regulatory and commercial use, continued publication, and leadership’s stated intention to retain market-moving reports.

These rubric ratings are **not numerical probabilities of disappearance**. They distinguish observed problems from emerging risks. “No Known Issue” means no qualifying problem was identified—not that preservation is guaranteed.

## 1. Historical Data Availability

| **Gone** | **Not supported.** Historical observations remain publicly accessible. |
| **High Risk** | **Not supported by the checks performed.** I did not identify removed historical inventory files or periods. This was not an exhaustive checksum comparison of every historical artifact. |
| **Moderate Risk** | **Not supported as a data-element removal finding.** Older regional definitions differ, but the legacy three-region series remains separately available. Ordinary revisions are documented, not evidence of suppression. |
| **No Known Issue** | **Supported.** EIA’s [legacy Lower 48 history](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/ng/hist/nw_epg0_sao_r48_bcfw.htm) still exposes observations beginning December 31, 1993. Thus, **latest-revised history is available, but a complete immutable archive of every original release vintage has not been established**. Legitimate revisions should not be confused with destructive alteration, but they make independent versioned preservation important.

**Confidence:** Moderate—strong spot-check evidence, but no comprehensive file-by-file integrity audit.

## Preservation implications

**The evidence points more strongly to operational disruption and product restructuring than to deliberate deletion of WNGSR.** Its market importance and federal regulatory use provide meaningful protection, but cannot eliminate staffing or IT risk.

Priority actions:

1. **Archive every release vintage**, including its actual publication time.
2. Preserve historical inventories, uncertainty measures, revisions, methodology, and legacy regions.
3. Keep independent copies: EIA’s HTML, downloads, and API are multiple interfaces, **not necessarily independent preservation systems**.
4. Monitor the **July 31, 2027 ICR expiration**, changes to EIA-912/EIA-191, release delays, and final staffing figures.
5. Reassess promptly if confirmed losses reach 40%, weekly releases are skipped, or regional/uncertainty fields disappear.
